name: Ship of Theseus
summary: A classical paradox of identity asking whether an object whose every part has been gradually replaced remains the same object.
explanation:
The Ship of Theseus is a thought experiment about identity and persistence over time, originating in classical antiquity and recorded by the Greek historian Plutarch. According to the story, the ship on which the hero Theseus returned to Athens was preserved by the Athenians, who replaced its decaying wooden planks one by one as they wore out. Eventually every original plank had been swapped for a new one, prompting philosophers to ask whether the vessel remained the same ship.

The puzzle challenges our intuitions about what makes a thing the same thing across change. On one view, identity is preserved because the ship maintains continuous form and function throughout the gradual replacement, so it is still Theseus's ship. On another view, identity depends on material composition, so once none of the original matter remains, it is a numerically different object that merely resembles the original.

The philosopher Thomas Hobbes sharpened the paradox by adding a twist. Suppose someone collects all the discarded original planks and reassembles them into a ship. Now there appear to be two ships, each with a claim to being the original, one preserving continuity and the other preserving the original material. They cannot both be identical to the first ship, which forces us to clarify what identity really tracks.

The problem has wide application beyond ships. Human bodies replace their cells over time, organizations retain their identity while every employee changes, and rivers persist though their water constantly flows away. It underlies questions of personal identity, the continuity of institutions and nations, and even legal and ethical questions about ownership and responsibility across change.

Philosophers respond to the paradox in various ways, distinguishing qualitative identity, being exactly similar, from numerical identity, being one and the same thing, and appealing to notions such as spatiotemporal continuity, essential properties, or the idea that identity is partly a matter of how we choose to individuate objects. The Ship of Theseus endures because it exposes how much our ordinary talk of sameness depends on assumptions we rarely examine.
